_about: Second Mate (FG) orals: 64 questions WRITTEN BY AptRun (AI-assisted), not taken from the Merchant Navy team's document, to bring every function to 230 questions so each set can be 10 + 10 + 10. Every one is imported with origin=generated and needs_review=true: a master mariner must check each answer before it is relied on. Edit here, then re-run build_merchant_navy.py and the seeder.

questions.q: What are the Master's Standing Orders and why must every OOW read them?
questions.a: Permanent written instructions from the Master on how the ship is to be navigated and when he must be called, such as minimum CPA, restricted visibility, equipment failure and traffic; every OOW reads and signs them and follows them on every watch.

questions.q: What must be recorded in the deck logbook during a navigational watch?
questions.a: Positions and times, courses and speeds, alterations of course, weather and visibility, compass errors, steering and equipment tests, pilot embarkation, significant traffic and events, and any call to the Master, written factually and signed.

questions.q: What is a Bridge Navigational Watch Alarm System (BNWAS) and how does it work?
questions.a: It monitors the alertness of the OOW: if it is not reset within the set period it gives a visual alarm, then an audible alarm on the bridge, then calls other officers or the Master, to warn that the OOW may be incapacitated. It must not be switched off at sea.

questions.q: What is an Under-Keel Clearance (UKC) policy and what does it take into account?
questions.a: A company or Master's policy fixing the minimum clear water that must remain beneath the keel. It allows for static draft, squat, heel, wave response, tide and the accuracy of the charted depths.

questions.q: What is the Cross-Track Distance (XTD) limit and how is it set?
questions.a: The maximum distance the ship may stray from her planned track on either side before she is in danger. It is set from the edge of the no-go areas, the accuracy of the position fixing and the ship's manoeuvrability, and is marked on the chart and ECDIS.

questions.q: How are navigational warnings such as NAVTEX and NAVAREA messages used in passage planning?
questions.a: They are collected during appraisal and throughout the voyage, assessed for their effect on the route, plotted on the chart or ECDIS as hazards, and the Master is told about any that affect the plan.

questions.q: How is gyro compass error found at sea?
questions.a: Compare the gyro bearing of the Sun or another body, or of two charted objects in transit, with the true bearing calculated or charted. Gyro error is true minus gyro bearing: gyro least, error east; gyro best, error west.

questions.q: What is the off-heading alarm on an autopilot?
questions.a: An alarm that sounds when the ship's heading differs from the set course by more than a preset number of degrees, warning the OOW that she is not holding her course. Its limit must be set sensibly and it must never be disabled.

questions.q: How is the magnetic compass checked against the gyro compass?
questions.a: At regular intervals, at least once every watch when possible, the magnetic reading is compared with the gyro heading after applying variation and deviation. A difference larger than expected shows an error in one of them, which must be investigated.

questions.q: What are CPA and TCPA?
questions.a: CPA is the Closest Point of Approach, the smallest distance at which a target will pass own ship if both keep course and speed. TCPA is the Time to that Closest Point of Approach. ARPA calculates both from the tracked target's vector.

questions.q: What is the difference between relative motion and true motion radar displays?
questions.a: Relative motion keeps own ship fixed on the screen and shows targets moving relative to her, which is best for judging risk of collision. True motion shows own ship and targets moving at their true courses and speeds over the ground or sea, which shows what each is actually doing.

questions.q: What is sea clutter and how do you reduce it?
questions.a: Unwanted echoes from wave crests near the ship. Reduce it with the sea clutter (STC) control, which cuts the gain at short range, and use the rain clutter (FTC) control for rain. Adjust carefully, because too much can hide small targets.

questions.q: What does Rule 8 require of action taken to avoid collision?
questions.a: The action must be positive, made in ample time and with due regard to good seamanship. Alterations of course or speed should be large enough to be readily apparent to another vessel observing visually or by radar, avoiding a succession of small alterations, and their effect must be checked until the other vessel is finally past and clear.

questions.q: What must the give-way vessel do under Rule 16?
questions.a: Take early and substantial action to keep well clear of the stand-on vessel.

questions.q: To which vessels does Rule 19 apply and what must they do?
questions.a: It applies to vessels not in sight of one another when navigating in or near an area of restricted visibility. Every vessel must proceed at a safe speed adapted to the circumstances, with her engines ready for immediate manoeuvre.

questions.q: What lights does a power-driven vessel of less than 50 metres show when underway?
questions.a: A masthead light forward, sidelights and a sternlight. A second masthead light abaft the first is optional on a vessel of less than 50 metres.

questions.q: What lights and shape does a vessel at anchor display?
questions.a: By night an all-round white light in the fore part, and a second all-round white light lower at the stern if she is 50 metres or more in length. By day one black ball in the fore part.

questions.q: What lights does a sailing vessel show when underway?
questions.a: Sidelights and a sternlight. A vessel under 20 metres may combine them in one tricolour lantern at the masthead, and any sailing vessel may add two all-round lights at the masthead, red over green.

questions.q: Describe the lateral marks of IALA Region A.
questions.a: Port-hand marks are red, can-shaped with a red cylinder topmark and a red light. Starboard-hand marks are green, conical with a green cone topmark pointing up and a green light, when proceeding in the direction of buoyage, which is entering from seaward.

questions.q: What is a leading line (transit) and how is it used?
questions.a: Two charted marks, such as lights or beacons, that when kept in line define a safe track. Keeping the rear mark above the front mark keeps the ship on the line, and a transit is also used to check compass error.

questions.q: What precautions are taken when embarking a pilot at sea?
questions.a: Rig the pilot ladder as required, on the lee side, in good condition and well lit, with a lifebuoy with light and a heaving line ready. A responsible officer in contact with the bridge meets the pilot, and speed is reduced and a lee made as agreed with the pilot boat.

questions.q: What corrections are applied to a sextant altitude of the Sun?
questions.a: Index error first, then dip for height of eye to give apparent altitude, then the main correction for refraction, semi-diameter and parallax to give true altitude. For a star there is no semi-diameter correction.

questions.q: What is a position line and how is a fix obtained from position lines?
questions.a: A line along which the ship must lie at the time of observation, obtained from a bearing, a distance, a depth contour or a celestial observation. Two or more position lines that cross give a fix, and three lines forming a cocked hat show how accurate it is.

questions.q: What is the intercept (Marcq St Hilaire) method?
questions.a: Compare the observed altitude of a body with the altitude calculated for an assumed position. The difference is the intercept, towards or away from the body, plotted along the azimuth from the assumed position, and the position line is drawn at right angles to it.

questions.q: What weather does a cold front bring?
questions.a: A cold front is where cold air advances under warmer air. It brings a sudden veer of the wind, a rapid rise of pressure after it passes, heavy showers or squalls from cumulonimbus cloud, a drop in temperature and good visibility behind it.

questions.q: What weather does a warm front bring?
questions.a: Warm air rises over retreating cold air. Cirrus thickens to nimbostratus with continuous rain, pressure falls and the wind backs ahead of the front, then the wind veers with warmer, damp air and poor visibility behind it.

questions.q: What is a squall and what is a line squall?
questions.a: A squall is a sudden sharp increase in wind speed lasting a few minutes, often with rain. A line squall is a line of squalls along a cold front, with a sudden veer of wind, a fall in temperature and a rise in pressure.

questions.q: What are your actions if the steering gear fails?
questions.a: Call the Master and the engine room, show the not-under-command lights or shapes, reduce speed or stop the engines as needed, change over to the emergency or auxiliary steering, warn other traffic by VHF and sound signals, and take avoiding action.

questions.q: What does a Mayday distress message contain?
questions.a: Mayday three times, this is, the ship's name three times, call sign or MMSI, then Mayday and the ship's name, the position, the nature of the distress, the assistance required and any other useful information such as the number of persons on board.

questions.q: What do you do on receiving a DSC distress alert?
questions.a: Listen on the distress channel, write down the position and details, tell the Master and plot the position. Do not acknowledge by DSC straight away; if no coast station acknowledges within a few minutes and you can help, acknowledge by radiotelephone and relay the alert if needed.

questions.topic: General Cargo Operations, Stowage & Mate's Receipts
questions.q: What is a stowage plan and why is it important?
questions.a: A plan showing where each parcel is stowed, with weights, ports of discharge and any special cargo. It ensures good stability and trim, acceptable stresses, segregation, and a sensible discharge sequence, and it is used by the stevedores and the next port.

questions.topic: General Cargo Operations, Stowage & Mate's Receipts
questions.q: What are the main principles of good cargo stowage?
questions.a: Safety of the ship and crew, safety of the cargo, rapid and economical loading and discharging, and full use of the ship's capacity. They are met by good stability and trim, correct distribution of weight, segregation of incompatible cargoes and proper securing.

questions.topic: General Cargo Operations, Stowage & Mate's Receipts
questions.q: What is a Letter of Indemnity and why is a Master cautious about accepting one?
questions.a: A written promise by a shipper or charterer to compensate the shipowner if a clean bill of lading is issued for cargo that is damaged or was not checked. It does not bind third parties or protect against fraud, so the Master should not issue a clean bill of lading for defective cargo and should consult the P&I Club.

questions.topic: Dry Bulk Cargoes & IMSBC Operational Principles
questions.q: Why must the Master consult the individual cargo schedule in the IMSBC Code before loading?
questions.a: Each schedule gives the properties and hazards of that cargo, how to stow and trim it, segregation, ventilation, precautions during the voyage and emergency procedures, so the cargo can be carried safely.

questions.topic: Dry Bulk Cargoes & IMSBC Operational Principles
questions.q: How are cargo holds prepared before loading a bulk cargo?
questions.a: Sweep and wash the holds as required, dry them, remove loose rust scale and old cargo residues and any odour, test the bilges and cover them, check hatch covers and fittings, and obtain acceptance from the surveyor at the cleanliness the charter party and cargo require.

questions.topic: Dry Bulk Cargoes & IMSBC Operational Principles
questions.q: What is the danger of loading a bulk cargo in the rain?
questions.a: Rain raises the moisture content, which can damage the cargo and, for a Group A cargo, move it towards the flow moisture point and liquefaction. Stop loading, close the hatch covers, resume only when dry and record it in the Statement of Facts.

questions.topic: High-Risk Bulk Commodities (Coal, Iron Ore, Concentrates)
questions.q: What are the hazards of carrying charcoal in bulk?
questions.a: Self-heating and spontaneous combustion, oxygen depletion in the hold and the release of carbon monoxide. The cargo must be properly prepared and the hold atmosphere monitored, and nobody may enter without proper enclosed space precautions.

questions.topic: High-Risk Bulk Commodities (Coal, Iron Ore, Concentrates)
questions.q: What are the hazards of carrying fishmeal?
questions.a: Self-heating and spontaneous combustion, oxygen depletion and toxic gas. The cargo must be treated with an antioxidant, the temperature monitored, and hatches kept closed unless the schedule says otherwise.

questions.topic: High-Risk Bulk Commodities (Coal, Iron Ore, Concentrates)
questions.q: What are the hazards of carrying ferrosilicon?
questions.a: It can give off flammable hydrogen and toxic phosphine or arsine gas when it gets wet, so it must be kept dry. Holds must be ventilated as the schedule requires and the atmosphere checked before entry.

questions.q: What is a Grain Loading Plan and who approves it?
questions.a: A plan showing how each hold is filled, trimmed and secured, with the calculated heeling moments. It is approved by the flag administration or its recognised organisation and carried on board with the Document of Authorization.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a shifting board in a grain hold?
questions.a: A longitudinal division fitted in the hold, from the deck down, that reduces the free surface of the grain and so limits the heeling moment if the cargo shifts.

questions.q: Why must grain be trimmed into the ends and under the deck beams?
questions.a: To fill every void so the grain cannot shift into empty space. A compartment trimmed full is treated as filled in the calculation, which gives a much smaller heeling moment.

questions.q: Why are heavier containers stowed lower in a stack?
questions.a: To keep the centre of gravity low for stability, to stay within the stack weight limits and so limit the load on lashings and corner posts, as the Cargo Securing Manual requires.

questions.q: Why is a wrongly declared container weight dangerous?
questions.a: Wrong weights make stability and stack weight calculations unreliable, can overload lashings, cranes and lifting gear, and can cause a stack to collapse or containers to be lost overboard, which is why the Verified Gross Mass is required.

questions.q: What is the bridge visibility requirement when containers are stowed on deck?
questions.a: The view of the sea surface from the conning position must not be blocked forward of the bow by more than two ship lengths or 500 metres, whichever is less, and the blind sectors must be limited in total and in size.

questions.q: What are the EmS schedules?
questions.a: The IMDG Emergency Schedules: for each UN number an F schedule for fire and an S schedule for spillage, giving the emergency response, used together with the Medical First Aid Guide.

questions.q: What is the Medical First Aid Guide (MFAG)?
questions.a: A guide giving first aid and medical treatment for people poisoned by, or in contact with, dangerous goods; it is used with the IMDG Code and the ship's medical guide.

questions.q: How are packages of dangerous goods marked and labelled?
questions.a: Each package shows the proper shipping name, the UN number, the hazard class label and the marine pollutant mark where it applies, and a container carries placards on all four sides.

questions.topic: Lifting Gear, Derricks, Cranes & Rope/Wire Care
questions.q: What safety precautions apply when using a ship's crane?
questions.a: Check the crane and its safe working load and radius, agree clear signals between the signalman and operator, keep people clear of the load, never lift above the safe working load or pull the load sideways, allow for ship movement, and secure the crane after use.

questions.topic: Lifting Gear, Derricks, Cranes & Rope/Wire Care
questions.q: How should wire rope be lubricated, stored and inspected?
questions.a: Clean off dirt and apply a suitable dressing regularly, store it dry on a reel or coiled in a ventilated place, avoid kinks and sharp bends, and inspect for broken wires, corrosion, flattening and loss of diameter.

questions.topic: Lifting Gear, Derricks, Cranes & Rope/Wire Care
questions.q: What are the hazards of lifting operations in rough weather and what do you do?
questions.a: Wind makes the load swing, ship movement adds dynamic loading and wet gear loses grip. Stop or restrict the lift when the crane's wind limit or the company procedure is reached, and secure the gear.

questions.topic: Oil Tanker Operations, Inert Gas & COW Concepts
questions.q: What are the hazards of a cargo pump room and how is it made safe?
questions.a: Flammable and toxic gas and lack of oxygen. It is ventilated mechanically before entry, tested for gas and oxygen, entered only under an enclosed space permit, and fitted with gas detection and bilge alarms.

questions.topic: Oil Tanker Operations, Inert Gas & COW Concepts
questions.q: What precautions prevent fire and explosion when handling flammable cargo?
questions.a: No smoking or naked lights, control of all ignition sources, hot work only with a permit, doors and ports closed, the ship and shore safety checklist agreed, firefighting equipment ready, and precautions against static electricity.

questions.topic: Oil Tanker Operations, Inert Gas & COW Concepts
questions.q: What is Reid Vapour Pressure?
questions.a: The pressure at which a liquid is in equilibrium with its vapour, measured at 37.8 degrees Celsius, used as an indication of how volatile a petroleum product is.

questions.q: What is a Threshold Limit Value and why does it matter on a chemical tanker?
questions.a: The airborne concentration of a substance to which workers can be exposed day after day, as a time-weighted average, without harm. It decides the gas testing limits and the breathing protection needed.

questions.q: What precautions apply when loading a toxic cargo on a chemical tanker?
questions.a: Closed loading with vapour return, a closed gauging system, protective clothing and breathing apparatus ready, vapour detection, a decontamination shower and eye wash, and a ship and shore agreement.

questions.q: How is cargo contamination prevented on a chemical tanker?
questions.a: Use segregated piping and pumps, close valves and fit blanks, check the compatibility chart and previous cargo, clean and inspect the tanks, test with a wall wash where needed, and make sure lines and hoses are clean and empty.

questions.topic: Hatch Covers, Ballast Management & Cargo Space Inspections
questions.q: What is the Ballast Water Record Book and how long is it kept?
questions.a: A record of every ballast operation, intake, discharge, exchange, treatment and accidental discharge, with dates, positions and volumes, signed by the officer in charge. It is kept on board for two years and then by the company for three years.

questions.topic: Hatch Covers, Ballast Management & Cargo Space Inspections
questions.q: What checks are made on the hatch covers before sailing?
questions.a: Every cleat is secured, rubber packing is inspected, drain channels and non-return valves are clear, covers are locked in position, and weathertightness is confirmed. A hatch left unsecured lets in green water.

questions.topic: Hatch Covers, Ballast Management & Cargo Space Inspections
questions.q: How are cargo residues and hold washings dealt with under MARPOL Annex V?
questions.a: Residues and washings that are not harmful to the marine environment may be discharged outside special areas under the Annex V conditions, while harmful ones must go to port reception facilities. Everything is recorded in the Garbage Record Book.

questions.q: What is the fluid GM and why must it be used?
questions.a: The solid GM less the virtual rise of G caused by free surface, which is the free surface moment divided by displacement. Fluid GM is the true stability of the ship and must be used for every stability check.

questions.q: What is a hydrostatic release unit?
questions.a: A device that automatically releases a liferaft or an EPIRB so it floats free if the ship sinks, operating at a shallow depth under water pressure. It must be serviced and renewed within its stated life.

questions.q: What is the Garbage Management Plan?
questions.a: A plan for collecting, storing, processing and disposing of garbage, including the use of equipment, with a person named in charge. It is required on ships of 100 gross tonnage and above, crew are trained in it, and placards are displayed on ships of 12 metres and over.

questions.topic: ISM, ISPS, MLC, STCW, Port State Control & Maritime Law
questions.q: What is the Master's overriding authority under the ISM Code?
questions.a: The company must state in the safety management system that the Master has the overriding authority and responsibility to make decisions on safety and pollution prevention and to ask the company for help whenever it is needed.
